title: Driving Video Retrieval for Complex Queries with Structured Grounding
claim: Embedding-based retrieval misses fine-grained temporal dynamics; explicitly modeling structured state changes retrieves the correct events.
layout: 2 stacked horizontal bands, query on top, three results per row, ✗/✓ verdicts
description: A query banner at the top, with a magnifier icon, reads 'Find videos where a vehicle changing lane in front of the ego vehicle.' Below are two stacked rounded bands. The top blue band is 'Traditional Retrieval (Embedding-based)' with the formula Sim(q,v)=cos(e_q,e_v). It shows three dashcam frames labeled Result 1–3 with captions describing wrong matches: the car stays in its lane, a car crosses an intersection, a vehicle comes from the opposite lane. A red ✗ says 'Fails on fine-grained motion.' The bottom peach band is 'Our Method (Structured Grounded)' with Sim(q,v)=f(J_v,r_q). It shows three dashcam frames, each topped by a small time-series plot of Δx(t) or Δlane(t) with spikes. A green ✓ says 'Captures temporal state change.' The eye goes first to the query, then to the blue-versus-peach contrast.
caption: Advantages of our method. Embedding-based retrieval captures global scene similarity but often ignores short-term motion dynamics, such as lane changing and hard braking. Our structured grounding method explicitly models these motion patterns, enabling accurate retrieval of such events.
abstract: Video retrieval at scale is central to data curation and safety validation in autonomous driving, where users want to find not only scenes but also dynamic events such as cut-ins and hard braking. Existing vision-language and keyword-based retrieval methods often miss these events because the relevant motion may not be explicitly described in text or captured by lexical overlap. Rule-based retrieval can encode such events more directly, but it is brittle: generated or hand-written rules often fail when their assumptions do not match real driving data. We propose STRIVE-D, a data-calibrated retrieval framework for driving videos. It uses weakly labeled in-domain videos to estimate when a query rule is reliable, adapt rules that mismatch observed data, and fuse calibrated rule scores with vision-language and keyword-based retrieval signals. Across three driving benchmarks, including newly released human-annotated event data on DrivingDojo, STRIVE-D delivers up to 84% relative improvement in top-1 accuracy over state-of-the-art methods.
